claims: A filibuster is a U.S. Senate procedural tactic used by a minority party to delay or block a vote on legislation by extending debate.
A filibuster requires a 60-vote supermajority known as cloture to end debate and proceed to a vote.
Historically, filibusters involved long speeches called "talking filibuster".
The modern "stealth" filibuster involves a senator threatening to filibuster.
A senator threatening to filibuster forces the Senate to secure 60 votes to invoke cloture.
Senate rules require a cloture motion to end debate.
A cloture motion requires 3/5ths of all senators.
A cloture motion typically requires 60 votes.
If the cloture motion fails, the bill is stalled.
Budget reconciliation bills cannot be filibustered.
Many executive branch nominations cannot be filibustered.
Federal judicial appointments cannot be filibustered.
Budget reconciliation bills, many executive branch nominations, and federal judicial appointments can pass with a simple majority.
Senator Strom Thurmond set the record for the longest filibuster in 1957 by speaking for 24 hours and 18 minutes against the Civil Rights Act, according to Wikipedia.
The filibuster emerged in the 1850s from a desire for unlimited debate.
U.S. Senate rules were tightened in 1917 introducing cloture.
The cloture vote requirement was changed to 60 votes in 1975, as noted in U.S. Senate (.gov) records.
